newsitem.title: UK: Precious Metals Outlook - Gold vulnerable to more losses.
newsitem.headline: Precious Metals Outlook - Gold vulnerable to more losses.

text.p: Gold was on shaky ground on Monday after a brisk, fund-driven rally last week ran into a technical brick wall and ended up in a major sell-off, analysts said.
But a solid base of support was emerging at gold's recent lows, which was likely to prevent more dramatic drops in the near term, they added.

"A quite interesting pattern is developing, in that gold is beginning to find support after making fresh lows all the way down since the peak at the start of the year," said technical analyst Susan Rigg of Chart Analysis Ltd.
Gold bounced off lows just under $377 in early October and November, and more recently has found support around $379.00.
Bullion closed in London on Friday at $379.50/$380.00 an ounce, down from the week's high of $384.70.
Still, gold needed to break decisively above the tough resistance which rebuffed last week's rise, analysts said.
"We may have to go through a ranging, support-building phase before going through the peak area of $384.50," Rigg said.

Prices had rallied steadily last week, starting on Monday after investment funds apparently realised that gold's floor around $376-$377 was going to hold and began to buy the metal, anticipating a run-up in prices.
But after selling from producers thwarted the rally, the funds abandoned the new stance and prices rapidly tumbled on Friday morning to close to the week's starting point.
Market mood was sharply divided on gold's next move, with some dealers predicting a retest of recent lows and others expecting a period of consolidation before a gradual climb.
"If the $379 area breaks, it's definitely going to go lower to at least $377," one London-based dealer said.
"But personally, I think it's found it's near-term floor and we're going to see $382, at least, by the end of this week."
With all eyes on gold, silver has been mostly rangebound in the $4.80-$4.95 area in the past several weeks, largely shrugging off gold's greater volatility.

"Silver has made some good upside progress, but it's proving less dynamic on the upside than gold and it really needs to push past the psychological $5.00 an ounce area if it's going to rise," analyst Rigg said.
Platinum was also seeking direction after closing on Friday at $384.00/$385 an ounce, down over $5.00 from the week's high.

Its bid to shoot higher last week toppled along with gold, despite a moderately bullish Platinum 1996 Interim Review from refiner Johnson Matthey, which forecast that world supplies of platinum would fall by 140,000 ounces this year.
Palladium similarly came off its highs to finish the week at $118.00/$119.00, down from highs above $120 an ounce.
